channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: EY nudged up its 2026 UK growth forecast to about 0.9% assuming the Strait of Hormuz reopens by autumn but warned of a possible 2027 contraction if it stays shut, as markets now expect a US Federal Reserve rate hike by year-end.
item.description:
The growth outlook is increasingly hostage to the war. EY raised its UK 2026 forecast to around 0.9% on its base case that the Strait of Hormuz reopens by end-September, with growth of 1.2% in 2027 — but its downside scenario, in which the strait stays closed into 2027, would slow 2026 growth to 0.5% and tip the UK into a 0.2% contraction in 2027, driven by an inflation surge from disrupted oil and gas. Rate expectations are firming with the energy shock: markets now expect the US Federal Reserve to raise rates by a quarter point by the end of 2026. Against the caution, a note of long-term confidence: JPMorgan pledged to inject over USD 750 billion into the US housing market by 2035, lifting mortgage lending more than 40% to help 500,000 households buy homes.

Industry Impact

The forecasts underline that the single biggest macro variable for chemical demand right now is whether the Iran war and Hormuz closure end soon: a reopening supports a modest recovery, while a prolonged closure means recession risk and renewed inflation across Europe. Firmer expectations of higher-for-longer interest rates keep the cost of capital elevated for capacity and decarbonisation projects. JPMorgan's housing commitment is a longer-dated positive for US construction-linked demand — coatings, adhesives, sealants and insulation materials.

The Economic Times | The Independent | The Independent | Commercial Times | Handelsblatt

item.title: Intel's EMIB-T packaging technology is drawing attention as TSMC's advanced-packaging capacity stays tight, Taiwan named an advanced-packaging lead expert, and the Kumamoto earthquake's aftermath continues to pressure Japan's chip and auto supply.
item.description:
The bottleneck in chipmaking has moved downstream to advanced packaging — the step that stitches chips together for AI and high-performance computing. With TSMC's CoWoS packaging capacity in long-term shortage, Intel's rival EMIB-T technology is drawing industry attention: reports put its yield near 90% at roughly half the cost of CoWoS, though it still faces adoption hurdles. The Global Electronics Association named a veteran semiconductor-packaging expert as its advanced-packaging technology lead for Taiwan, underscoring the region's push to deepen its edge. Adding supply-side strain, the aftermath of the magnitude-7 Kumamoto earthquake continues to disrupt Japan's semiconductor and auto industries, keeping regional chip supply tight even as demand from AI stays intense.

Industry Impact

Advanced packaging is a fast-growing, materials-intensive frontier for ACS: it relies on specialty adhesives, underfills, thermal-interface materials, encapsulants and dielectric chemistries. Persistent packaging shortages and the race between TSMC and Intel packaging platforms both raise demand for these materials and reward suppliers that can qualify into new packaging processes. Continued Japanese supply disruption reinforces the case, seen throughout recent runs, for diversifying electronic-materials sourcing away from single geographic clusters.

Chinatimes | Global Electronics Association | Bjd.com.cn

item.title: Brazil's 80-year-old President Lula launched his fourth-term campaign and was formally nominated by his party, but a new poll shows Flavio Bolsonaro drawing nearly level, as the central bank prepares a fourth straight interest-rate cut.
item.description:
Brazil's October election is shaping up as a close contest. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, 80, said he was "in great shape" as he launched his bid for a fourth and final term, and the ruling Workers' Party formally nominated him, pairing him again with Vice President Alckmin. But a Nexus/BTG Pactual poll released on 3 August showed Senator Flavio Bolsonaro closing the gap: in a simulated runoff Lula led just 46% to 45%, narrower than the previous 47%–43%. On the economy, the central bank is expected to cut its benchmark Selic rate for a fourth straight meeting on 5 August, extending a cautious easing cycle that has brought rates down from a near-two-decade high of 15% to 14.25%.

Industry Impact

Brazil is a priority Latin American market (agriculture, autos, construction, consumer goods) and political direction shapes the investment and trade climate for chemical demand there. A tight race raises policy uncertainty into the autumn, while the easing rate cycle is supportive for construction and industrial activity — and therefore for coatings, adhesives and agricultural chemistries. Firms with Brazilian exposure should watch the election trajectory and the pace of monetary easing as the key swing variables for demand.

South China Morning Post | MarketScreener | China Daily | MarketScreener

item.title: Germany's leaders vowed to make the country "war-ready" within years and Japan is investing trillions of yen to rebuild its defence industry, as the White House moved to purge Chinese materials from the US defence supply chain.
item.description:
Rearmament is reshaping industrial policy across the democracies. Germany's Chancellor Merz and Defence Minister Pistorius declared a goal of making Germany "war-ready" within a few years, though the Bundeswehr remains far from its target of 260,000 active soldiers by the mid-2030s. Japan is channelling trillions of yen into transforming its defence industry into a "core national power," easing arms-export limits and backing defence start-ups and SMEs amid perceived threats from China, North Korea and Russia. At the Farnborough Airshow, Boeing showcased its Ghost Bat unmanned fighter — expected to cost less than a third of an F-35 — reflecting a broader shift toward autonomous systems. And the White House signed an executive order removing the "exceptional circumstances" waiver that had allowed continued use of Chinese tungsten in the US defence supply chain, with the exemption ending from 2027.

Industry Impact

Sustained defence spending is a growing demand pool for specialty chemicals and materials — structural adhesives, coatings, composites, propellant and electronics chemistries used in aircraft, vehicles and munitions. The drive to purge Chinese critical materials (tungsten, and by extension other strategic inputs) from Western defence chains will reshape sourcing and could tighten supply and raise prices for affected materials, while creating openings for non-Chinese suppliers. Japan's easing of export rules signals a larger, more open defence-industrial market to serve.

Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung | The Straits Times | Commercial Times | MarketScreener

item.title: China's planning agency is urgently drafting a 2026–30 strategy to expand domestic demand and economists see room for rate and reserve-ratio cuts, while global consumer giants reported strong China sales despite a sluggish retail market.
item.description:
Beijing is moving to shore up demand. The National Development and Reform Commission said it is urgently drafting the implementation plan for a 2026–30 strategy to expand domestic demand, tying consumption support to livelihood improvements. UBS's chief China economist said policymakers still have room to cut interest rates and the reserve requirement ratio (the share of deposits banks must hold in reserve) in coming months to lower financing costs, deployed flexibly as data warrant, as leaders prioritise a solid start to the 15th Five-Year Plan. Against the "sluggish retail" narrative, multinationals painted a more resilient picture: in the first half, Unilever and Coca-Cola reported strong China sales growth, L'Oréal grew across all categories, and Adidas's China sales rose 16%. China's total goods trade reached CNY 25.5 trillion in the first half. It is a mixed signal — official stimulus is ramping up precisely because underlying demand remains uneven.

Industry Impact

Chinese demand is a swing factor for global chemical volumes, and stimulus aimed at consumption and infrastructure supports coatings, adhesives, packaging and construction chemistries. Rate and reserve-ratio cuts would ease conditions for the property and manufacturing sectors that consume ACS products. The resilience of consumer-goods multinationals in China is a modestly positive read-through for packaging and consumer-linked materials, even as the broader retail market stays soft. Execution of the demand-expansion plan is the variable to watch.

China Economic Net | China Daily | South China Morning Post | China Economic Net

item.title: The US offered Saudi Arabia its F-35 stealth fighter, which would make the kingdom the first non-NATO buyer and deepen a defence tie that now sits alongside a civilian nuclear deal, even as Saudi Aramco called China a key long-term pillar.
item.description:
Washington offered Riyadh its most advanced fifth-generation stealth jet, the F-35 — a step that would make Saudi Arabia the first non-NATO country to receive it and cements a fast-deepening US–Saudi defence relationship that already includes the recently announced civilian nuclear cooperation. The offer has strategic ripples: India signalled it has no plans to buy the jet, and analysts note the regional balance implications. Yet Saudi Arabia is hedging, not choosing sides: Aramco Asia's president said the company still sees China as an important pillar of its long-term global strategy, with over CNY 20 billion committed to Chinese investment projects. Saudi Arabia's Yanbu oil port, meanwhile, recorded its busiest day since the Houthi blockade began, a sign the kingdom is working to keep crude flowing despite the war.

Industry Impact

The US–Saudi deepening reinforces the Gulf's shift from pure oil exporter toward a diversified industrial and defence economy — a long-run opportunity for construction, materials and industrial-chemical suppliers if the nuclear and defence programmes proceed. Saudi Arabia's simultaneous courting of both Washington and Beijing illustrates the multipolar sourcing environment chemical firms now operate in, where major buyers deliberately keep options open across rival blocs. Gulf port throughput is worth watching as a real-time gauge of whether regional energy and freight flows are normalising.

DNA | China Economic Net | AA

item.title: Extreme heat and drought across the Netherlands, Germany and Italy are drying rivers, endangering flood barriers, cutting shipping capacity and forcing power plants offline, while Landes in France reported summer-crop losses of up to 70%.
item.description:
A continent-wide drought is stressing infrastructure and agriculture. In the Netherlands — about a third of which sits below sea level — falling levels on the river Waal are drying riverbeds and raising the risk to flood barriers, keeping water authorities on alert. Italy's Po River Basin Authority raised its drought emergency to "high," with over 100 municipalities in Piedmont and Lombardy facing critical drinking-water shortages. Low water on the Danube forced Hungary's Paks nuclear plant to cut output — one of several European power stations constrained because rivers are too low or too warm to provide cooling. In France, the Landes agricultural chamber estimated the most intense July drought on record, with an 85% rainfall deficit and non-irrigated maize yields down 50–70%. Governments across Europe are scrambling with emergency measures to secure water, power and transport.

Industry Impact

Low water on the Rhine, Danube and other rivers is a direct and recurring threat to European chemical logistics, much of which moves by barge — expect freight surcharges, reduced load factors and rerouting through the dry season. Power constraints add operating-cost and reliability risk for energy-intensive chemical production. The crop losses feed agricultural-input and food-price pressure, supporting demand for crop-protection chemistries while raising costs for bio-based feedstocks. This is now a structural summer risk to plan around, not a one-off.

China Economic Net | Bjd.com.cn | Der Standard | Reussir

item.title: An Australian think-tank found China now leads the US in 69 of 74 critical and advanced technologies, and Alibaba and MiniMax released powerful new open-source AI models, even as China's state media warned against a "mad rush" into future industries.
item.description:
The Australian Strategic Policy Institute reported that China now leads the US in 69 of 74 technologies it classes as critical and advanced — from advanced materials to AI — calling it a "clear signal of a structural shift" in global technological power; China also makes about 90% of the world's humanoid robots. The momentum showed in AI: Alibaba unveiled Qwen3.8-Max, its most powerful model yet at 2.4 trillion parameters, and said it would release the weights so developers can run and adapt it; Chinese firm MiniMax open-sourced its multimodal H3 model with day-one support from 16 chipmakers including Intel, AMD and Huawei. Robotics and embodied AI dominated the World Artificial Intelligence Conference. But Beijing is wary of its own boom: the Economic Daily warned against "a mad rush and reckless spending" in future industries, noting nearly every province is piling into hydrogen, bio-manufacturing and embodied intelligence — a recipe for the kind of overcapacity that has hit solar and EVs.

Industry Impact

China's technology lead reshapes competition for the advanced-materials and electronics markets ACS producers supply. Open-source Chinese AI lowers the cost of automation and could accelerate adoption across manufacturing, a productivity opportunity for chemical operations. But the overcapacity warning is the flip side of the "China Shock" theme: a state-driven rush into new industries tends to flood global markets and compress margins, which is exactly the dynamic pressuring European producers. Watching which "future industries" get over-built helps anticipate the next wave of price competition.

The Sydney Morning Herald | WirtschaftsWoche | Global Times | Lianhe Zaobao | Xhby.net | Axios

item.title: A Deloitte study found 77% of the electric-car battery cells fitted in Europe in 2025 came from Asia, up from 70%, with Europe making just 13% and Asian firms controlling most of its capacity, as German premium carmakers sink into a profitability crisis.
item.description:
Europe's electric-vehicle industry is growing more dependent on Asia for its most valuable component. Consultancy Deloitte found that 77% of the battery cells installed in European e-cars in 2025 were made in Asia — up seven points from 2024 — while Europe accounts for only about 13% of production, and Asian companies control roughly 98% of European cell-manufacturing capacity. Deloitte warns European firms could forgo around EUR 10.5 billion in profit by 2030 if they cannot localise. The strategic weakness compounds a financial one: a Handelsblatt analysis of first-half results found profit margins in the core car business at BMW and Mercedes have in places fallen below those of mass-market makers, and a wider debate ("Is the German auto industry finished?") frames the slump as structural rather than cyclical. Chinese brands, meanwhile, keep gaining — one in four pure EVs registered in Spain this year was Chinese-made, with BYD overtaking Tesla there.

Industry Impact

Autos are a core ACS end-market (battery-assembly adhesives, structural bonding, sealants, coatings), so both the battery-dependence and the margin squeeze matter. Reliance on Asian cells means the fastest-growing value pool in EV production sits largely outside Europe, limiting where European ACS suppliers can attach. Thin OEM margins push cost pressure down the chain onto suppliers. The bright spot is that any European move to localise cell and battery-material production would create new demand for bonding, thermal and protective chemistries close to home.

Die Zeit | Yahoo Germany | Frankfurter Rundschau | Handelsblatt | Die Zeit | El Correo

item.title: US factory activity jumped to a four-year high in July while Taiwan, Japan and Singapore stayed strongly in expansion, but global manufacturing slowed overall as the Middle East war sapped demand and Europe barely grew.
item.description:
July's purchasing-managers' surveys (PMIs, where a reading above 50 signals expansion) showed a widening split. The US ISM manufacturing index surged 2.3 points to 55.6, its highest since 2022, with factory employment expanding for the first time in nearly three years. Asia's tech-linked economies led: Taiwan's PMI hit 61.5, its fastest in almost five years, Japan held at 54.5 (a seventh month of growth), Singapore rose to 51.4 with its electronics gauge at an eight-year high, and Indonesia climbed back above 50 to 50.2. But the global aggregate weakened: S&P Global reported China slipping and much of Europe stalling as the five-month Middle East war delivered weaker demand and higher costs. The eurozone managed only 51.9 and the UK slowed to 51.9, a four-month low. In short, an AI-and-defence-driven upswing in the US and Asian tech hubs is running against a war-driven slowdown in China and Europe.

Industry Impact

The divergence tells chemical producers where demand is: robust in US and Asian manufacturing (electronics, AI hardware, industrial goods) and soft in European and Chinese factories. For ACS suppliers it argues for tilting volume and inventory toward the expanding US and Taiwan/Japan/Singapore clusters while managing overcapacity risk in Europe. The strong US employment component also supports durable-goods and construction-linked demand, whereas the European readings reinforce the stagnation flagged in recent runs.

The Economic Times | The Straits Times | Commercial Times | Dünya | Lianhe Zaobao | Jakarta Post

item.title: Thailand and Canada launched a cement carbon-capture pilot, SGL Carbon agreed to double its output of nuclear-grade graphite, and a chemical accident at a GKN Aerospace plant strained aircraft supply chains as green steel reshapes raw-material demand.
item.description:
Several material-supply and decarbonisation moves converged. The Thai Cement Manufacturers Association, working with Canada, designated a "Saraburi Sandbox" to pilot carbon-capture technology in cement — one of the hardest sectors to decarbonise — bringing industry, government and academia together to cut emissions while protecting competitiveness. SGL Carbon and US reactor developer X-energy signed a binding deal to double SGL's capacity for medium-grain isotropic graphite (NBG-18), a critical, long-lead-time material for X-energy's high-temperature reactors, at SGL's site in Chedde, France; X-energy will fund equipment upgrades in milestone payments. The shift to low-emission "green" steel is separately pressuring traditional supply chains, forcing raw-material producers to rethink strategy toward purer inputs. And a chemical accident at a GKN Aerospace plant near Los Angeles — an overheated tank that risked exploding and forced 50,000 residents to evacuate — temporarily halted production and strained aircraft-makers' supply chains as the site works back to full capacity.

Industry Impact

These stories sit close to the ACS core. Cement and steel decarbonisation reshape demand for construction chemicals, admixtures and functional additives, and open markets for products that enable lower-carbon building materials. Specialty carbon and graphite tie into the electronics, battery and nuclear value chains where ACS players supply bonding and protective chemistries. The GKN incident is a reminder that single-site chemical disruptions can cascade through tightly-coupled aerospace supply chains — an argument for qualified second sources on critical process chemicals.

AP | Bizhub | AP | Wallstreet-online | Wallstreet-online | WirtschaftsWoche

item.title: Twenty-five Democratic-led US states sued in the trade court to block Trump's 10–12.5% "forced-labour" tariffs on 60 economies, arguing he exceeded his authority after the Supreme Court struck down his earlier tariffs, as fresh duties hit Pakistan.
item.description:
A coalition of 25 states — including California, New York and Hawaii — filed suit in the US Court of International Trade to overturn the latest tariffs, which took effect on 24 July and impose 10% or 12.5% duties on goods from about 60 economies, including the EU and China. The states argue the administration illegally stretched Section 301 of the 1974 Trade Act (a provision meant for targeted retaliation against unfair trade practices) to rebuild a broad tariff wall after the Supreme Court struck down Trump's earlier "reciprocal" tariffs in February. California filed a second, separate suit. The pressure is compounding: Washington added a 10% duty on top of Pakistan's existing 29% rate — a blow its textile exporters estimate at USD 564 million this year — and US steel imports have fallen almost 23% as the tariff wall reshapes trade flows. Earlier moves under Section 338 also hit Canadian goods. The legal challenge injects fresh uncertainty into whether the tariff regime survives intact.

Industry Impact

For globally sourced chemical and ACS supply chains, the lawsuit matters because it puts the durability of the whole tariff structure in doubt — a court loss could unwind duties that firms are already re-routing around, while a win entrenches them for years. Either way, the near-term reality is higher landed costs on EU- and Asia-sourced inputs and finished goods, and continued incentive to localise. Falling US steel imports show how quickly tariffs redirect trade, a pattern likely to repeat across chemical feedstocks and intermediates.

Politico | LiveMint | Le Figaro | Los Angeles Times | Dawn | BSSA

item.title: Hopes for a US–Iran peace deal pushed oil sharply lower and lifted Germany's Dax to a record after Trump paused a threatened major strike and said talks would begin, but the threat to oil tankers is now the worst since the war started.
item.description:
Markets swung toward relief. President Trump temporarily called off what he described as the US military's "largest attack since the Second World War" and said fresh talks with Iran would begin, prioritising diplomacy after days of escalation threats. Oil prices tumbled and European shares rose — Germany's Dax hit a record above 25,970 points. But the picture stayed fragile: Iran denied Trump's claim that it was negotiating to reopen the Strait of Hormuz (the sea lane carrying about a fifth of the world's oil), saying only that it was talking to Oman. Experts told the BBC the threat to oil tankers is now at its worst since the war began, after a string of attacks on the Red Sea route that some ships had used to bypass the blocked strait. The International Energy Agency's chief has called the war the "greatest threat to energy security" in modern history. Trump also lashed out at oil majors for "making too much money" — US pump prices are up more than 37% since the war began, and ExxonMobil's second-quarter profit more than doubled to USD 14.5 billion.

Industry Impact

For the Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants (ACS) industry, a genuine de-escalation would be the first real relief on input costs since February — lower crude eases naphtha, solvent and packaging prices and calms freight. But the reversal is only a hope, not a settlement: with Iran denying reopening talks and tanker risk peaking, buyers should treat the oil drop as tentative and keep hedges and buffer stocks in place until a Hormuz reopening is actually confirmed. Sustained high pump prices and fat oil-major margins also signal that the cost relief has not yet reached downstream chemical buyers.

Handelsblatt | MarketScreener | BBC News | New Indian Express | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung | AA
